activity_context.topic_title: Surface Areas of Revolution: Rotation About the Y-Axis

examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Surface Area of Revolution
examples.problem: Consider the segment of the line $y = 2x$ that lies between the lines $x = 0$ and $x = 2.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this segment is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis.
examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} x\sqrt{1 + \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2 = 4.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{5}[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}] \\  & =4\pi \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $y=5x-{x}^{3}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
feedback.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x-{x}^{3} & =0 \\ x(5-{x}^{2}) & =0 \\ x & =0,\pm \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=\sqrt{5}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x-{x}^{3})=5-3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}x\sqrt{1+{(5-3{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}x\sqrt{26-30{x}^{2}+9{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
